evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected small bowel obstruction in the emergency department, focusing on adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO). Verified against the WSES Bologna guidelines (2017 update). Large bowel obstruction (volvulus, colorectal cancer) is not covered by this source and needs its own pathway.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Drug and contrast doses — local protocol

pathophysiology.summary: Bowel obstruction blocks the passage of intestinal contents. Adhesions from previous surgery are the single most common cause of small bowel obstruction; others are incarcerated hernias, tumours, Crohn's disease and volvulus.
keyMechanisms: Proximal to the block, bowel distends with gas and fluid; vomiting and third-space losses cause dehydration, hypokalaemia and acute kidney injury.
Rising intraluminal pressure and twisting (closed loop) compromise venous then arterial flow → strangulation, ischaemia, perforation and peritonitis.
Examination detects strangulation in only about 48% of cases, so imaging and laboratory markers are essential.
Most adhesive obstructions (about 70–90%) settle with non-operative management; recurrence is common.

symptoms: Vomiting (early and bilious in proximal obstruction).
Constipation, absolute (no flatus) in complete obstruction.
physicalSigns: Distended, tympanic abdomen; scars of previous surgery.
Check all hernial orifices (groin and abdominal wall).
Dehydration: tachycardia, dry mucosa, low urine output.
Peritonitis (guarding, rigidity, constant pain), fever or shock suggest strangulation or perforation.
redFlags: Signs of strangulation or ischaemia — raised lactate, fever, tachycardia, shock
CT: closed loop, reduced bowel wall enhancement (ischaemia), free fluid

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Post-operative, electrolyte or drug-related; no transition point on CT.
Colonic dilatation on CT; different management.
Pain out of proportion to signs, high lactate; CT angiography.
Non-adhesive causes identified on CT — not managed as ASBO.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate and assess
actions: IV fluid resuscitation; correct electrolytes (especially potassium); monitor urine output.
Analgesia and antiemetic; nil by mouth.
Bloods: FBC, CRP, lactate, electrolytes, urea, creatinine. Check hernias.

clinicalManagement.title: CT with water-soluble contrast
actions: CT identifies cause and signs needing urgent surgery.
If ASBO is certain (other causes excluded on recent imaging) and no signs needing immediate surgery, a water-soluble contrast study alone is sufficient.

clinicalManagement.title: Decide: surgery now or non-operative trial
actions: Peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia (clinical, lactate or CT) → emergency surgery.
Lower threshold for early surgery in diabetes (higher AKI and MI risk when delayed more than 24 h); weigh frailty and quality of life.

clinicalManagement.title: Non-operative management
actions: Nil by mouth, NG (or long intestinal tube) decompression, fluids, electrolyte correction, nutritional support, aspiration prevention.
Water-soluble contrast with abdominal X-ray at 24 h: contrast in colon = resolving; no contrast = likely failure → surgery.
A 72-h non-operative trial is considered safe; operate if no resolution or any deterioration.

clinicalManagement.title: Operative management
actions: Laparotomy or carefully selected laparoscopic adhesiolysis (best for single band, few previous laparotomies).
Adhesion barriers reduce recurrence after operative treatment.

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute bowel obstruction in the emergency department.

keyPoints: CT with water-soluble contrast is the key test.
Otherwise NG decompression, fluids and electrolytes for up to 72 h.
Contrast in the colon at 24 h predicts success.
pitfalls: Relying on examination to exclude strangulation (sensitivity about 48%).
Prolonging non-operative treatment beyond 72 h without progress.

patientEducation: Recurrence risk after adhesive obstruction; seek care early with pain, vomiting or distension.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: Dietitian for nutritional support if prolonged nil by mouth.
dischargeCriteria: Obstruction resolved: passing flatus/stool, tolerating diet, NG removed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Explain recurrence risk; return if pain, vomiting or distension recur. Surgical follow-up after operative treatment.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Peritonitis, strangulation or bowel ischaemia (clinical, lactate, or CT: closed loop, ischaemia, free fluid)
ASBO without the above — up to 72 h
In colon = likely resolution; not in colon = likely failure

medicationPlan.note: The WSES Bologna guideline does not specify drug or contrast doses. Use local protocols for analgesia, antiemetics, fluids, electrolytes and water-soluble contrast volume.
